# Booth et al., secure development practices for generative AI and dual-use foundation models (NIST SP 800-218A)

**Source:** Harold Booth, Murugiah Souppaya, Apostol Vassilev, Michael Ogata, Martin Stanley and Karen Scarfone, *Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile*, NIST SP 800-218A, July 2024, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A. Not subject to copyright in the United States (Authority, PDF p. 3). Scope: open.
**Structure:** A 30-page NIST Special Publication. Front matter (PDF pp. 1–4, pp. i–iv), an Introduction (pp. 1–3), a section on using the Profile (pp. 4–5), and the Profile itself (pp. 6–19), whose Table 1 sets out 20 SSDF practices and 48 tasks (the deep reference's count of its rows; the Profile states no totals) in four groups (Prepare the Organization, Protect Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, Respond to Vulnerabilities), then 19 references (pp. 20–21) and a nine-term glossary (p. 22).

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The Profile is NIST's response to Section 4.1.a of Executive Order 14110, which tasked NIST with a companion resource to the Secure Software Development Framework covering secure development practices for generative AI and dual-use foundation models (p. 1). It augments SSDF version 1.1 (SP 800-218) with recommendations, considerations, notes and informative references specific to AI model development, documented as an SSDF Community Profile: a baseline of SSDF practices and tasks enhanced for a particular use case (p. 1). It supplements SP 800-218 and should not be used without it (p. 1).

AI models and systems inherit much of the same risk as any digital system, but the boundary between system code and system data blurs, people interact with the systems in plain language, and models, their parameters and the data they touch can form closed loops open to manipulation (p. 1). Development is still more art than exact science; training data may come from unknown or untrusted sources, weights can be tampered with, some models may be so complex that they cannot easily be thoroughly inspected, and crafted queries can yield objectionable output or injection-style attacks (p. 1). The Profile is a risk-based starting point, not a checklist, for AI model producers, AI system producers and AI system acquirers, whose responsibility for its practices may be shared; it covers cybersecurity risk only (pp. ii, 4–5).

## Purpose, Scope and Audiences

The scope is AI model development: data sourcing, designing, training, fine-tuning and evaluating models, and incorporating and integrating them into other software (p. 2). Consistent with SSDF 1.1 and EO 14110, practices for the deployment and operation of AI systems with AI models are out of scope, as is the data governance and management life cycle beyond cybersecurity practices for the data used in development (pp. 2, 8). The Profile does not distinguish human-written from AI-generated source code, on the assumption that all source code should be evaluated before use (p. 2). Readers should also use SP 800-218's own implementation examples and informative references, which apply generally to AI work (p. 1).

The three primary audiences are AI model producers (organisations developing their own generative AI and dual-use foundation models), AI system producers (organisations building software that leverages such a model) and AI system acquirers (organisations acquiring a product or service that uses AI systems); the terms follow SP 800-218's Audience statement (p. ii). Readers need not be experts, though implementing the practices may need expertise (p. ii). The document draws on NIST's trustworthy-AI work (the AI RMF, the adversarial machine learning taxonomy, the bias standard SP 1270 and the Dioptra testbed), the SSDF itself, NIST's general cybersecurity resources, and practitioners heard mainly at a January 2024 NIST workshop (pp. ii, 2).

## Using the Profile

Following SSDF practices should help model producers reduce vulnerabilities, reduce the potential impact of their exploitation and address root causes to prevent recurrence; system producers can use its vocabulary with model producers, and acquirers can use its terms to state cybersecurity requirements, for instance during acquisition (p. 4). Organisations should take a risk-based approach to deciding which practices and tasks are relevant, appropriate and effective from their own position (producer of models, producer of systems, or acquirer), weighing risk, cost, feasibility and applicability; cost models may need updating for AI work, and the risk-based approach may change as capabilities and risks change (p. 4). The document uses a general life cycle for consistency with SSDF 1.1 and invites adaptation to any machine learning-specific life cycle (p. 4).

Model versioning and lineage are harder to track: source code for a model's architecture and binaries is amenable to secure software engineering practices for versioning, lineage and reproducibility, but the final weights are defined only after training and fine-tuning, which is where tracking of collection, processing and training runs into limits (p. 4). Organisations should apply secure practices fully where they can, as far as possible elsewhere, and document the parts and artifacts the practices do not cover (p. 4). The practices can be integrated into MLOps in a CI/CD pipeline (p. 4).

When a model built by one organisation runs in a system hosted by a second and used by others, there is likely a shared responsibility model; an acquirer can set an agreement specifying which party is responsible for each practice and task and how each attests to conformance (pp. 4–5). The SSDF and the Profile address cybersecurity risk management only; privacy, intellectual property, bias and other risks should be managed along with cybersecurity risk as part of a mature enterprise risk management programme, and the Profile lists NIST resources for them (p. 5).

## How Table 1 Is Built

Table 1 gives, for each practice and task: its name, identifier and explanation; a suggested priority; recommendations [R], considerations [C] and notes [N] specific to AI model development; and informative references (pp. 6–7). Practices and tasks are unchanged from SSDF 1.1 unless tagged "Modified from SSDF 1.1" or "Not part of SSDF 1.1" (p. 6). An R is something the organisation should do, a C something it should consider doing, and an N additional information; appending the letter and number to the task ID gives a unique identifier, such as PO.1.2.R1 (p. 6). "No additions to SSDF 1.1" means the Profile adds nothing AI-specific to that task (p. 6). Organisations are expected to adapt, customise and omit items (p. 6).

Priority is a starting point for organisations to set their own: High is critically important for AI model development security compared with other tasks, Medium directly supports it, and Low benefits secure development but is generally no more important than most other tasks (p. 6). The informative references come from the AI RMF 1.0, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1 and NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy; the OWASP entries are identifiers only, with no names given (pp. 7–18). NIST is considering a future Implementation Examples column, giving options for the "how" where the existing column gives the "what" (p. 7). Numbering gaps are inherited: PW.4.3 was an SSDF 1.0 task moved elsewhere in 1.1, so its ID was not reused (p. 8).

## Prepare the Organization (PO)

The PO group's additions bring AI model development into an organisation's security requirements, roles, training, tooling and environments (pp. 8–11). Requirements should cover AI model development, AI model operations and data science, and AI model architectures and training techniques should be chosen in line with recommended practice for cybersecurity, privacy and reproducibility; reusing or expanding existing data classification policy is a consideration, and data, model and system cards are possible forms of model documentation (PO.1.1, PO.1.2, p. 8). Third-party component requirements should include AI model development security (PO.1.3, p. 8). Roles, responsibilities and role-based training should include AI model development security and threats to AI models; responsibilities shared with AI model producers, AI system producers and other providers can be set in agreements; leadership should commit to secure practices involving AI models (PO.2, p. 9).

Toolchains should be automated to secure AI model development at the scale AI models often use, ideally doing most of the work, with their security verified at a frequency commensurate with risk (PO.3.1, PO.3.2, p. 9). Tools should generate artifacts, such as attestations of the integrity and provenance of training datasets (PO.3.3, p. 10). Guardrails and controls should run throughout the AI development life cycle, beyond the traditional SDLC, with human-in-the-loop review considered for security checks past risk-based thresholds (PO.4.1, p. 10). Separating execution environments from each other as far as feasible is a consideration; resource use by model users should be limited, sensitive and production data kept in approved environments, pipelines and model registries protected by least privilege and continuously monitored, and environments watched for plaintext secrets (PO.5.1, pp. 10–11). A new task, PO.5.3, calls for continuous security monitoring of development components hosting AI models or related resources, with alerts when activity passes a risk threshold (p. 11).

## Protect Software (PS)

PS.1, tagged as modified from SSDF 1.1, covers both code and data (p. 11). Secure storage should include AI models, model weights, pipelines and reward models; direct access to models should be minimised, reward models stored apart, and only indirect access to weights permitted; preventing all human access to weights, and requiring all model development to happen in approved environments, are considerations (PS.1.1, pp. 11–12). Two new tasks protect training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data (PS.1.2) and model weights and configuration parameters (PS.1.3) from unauthorised access and modification, through continuous monitoring, separation of weights from data, least privilege, and risk-proportionate measures such as encryption, cryptographic hashes, digital signatures, multi-party authorisation and air-gapped environments (p. 12).

Acquirers should be given cryptographic hashes or digital signatures for a model, its components, artifacts and documentation, and signatures for model changes (PS.2.1, p. 12). Each release's archive should version the infrastructure tools that build datasets and train models, and record why the model was selected and how it was trained; models and their components may need adding to asset inventories (PS.3.1, pp. 12–13). Provenance should be tracked for models, their components and derivatives, and models trained on sensitive data should be tracked, deciding whether access should be restricted to people who already have access to that data; disclosing training-data provenance is a consideration (PS.3.2, p. 13).

## Produce Well-Secured Software (PW)

Risk modelling should include AI-specific vulnerability and threat types, which the Profile exemplifies, citing the adversarial machine learning taxonomy, as training-data poisoning, malicious content in inputs and outputs, denial of service from adversarial prompts, supply chain attacks, unauthorised disclosure, weight theft and data-pipeline misconfiguration; periodic updates for later model versions and derivatives, and a check that the AI model is not on a critical path for making significant security decisions without a human in the loop, are considerations (PW.1.1, pp. 13–14). PW.1.2, PW.1.3 and PW.2.1 carry no AI-specific additions (p. 14).

The new practice PW.3 confirms the integrity of training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data before use (pp. 14–15). Data is to be analysed for poisoning, bias, homogeneity and tampering, its provenance (when known) and integrity verified, and methods such as anomaly detection, bias detection, cleaning, curation, filtering, sanitisation, fact-checking and noise reduction applied, with human-in-the-loop examination considered (PW.3.1); provenance is tracked where known and unknown provenance documented (PW.3.2); and adversarial samples are included in training and testing under controls and guardrails (PW.3.3).

Using an existing model instead of building one is a consideration (PW.4.1, p. 15). Acquired models and components, including datasets, reward models, adaptation layers and configuration parameters, should be verified for integrity, provenance and security and scanned and tested before use (PW.4.4, pp. 15–16). Secure coding should cover AI-specific concerns: inputs (including prompts and user data) and outputs handled carefully, logged, analysed and validated in the model's context, sanitised or dropped when faulty, and encoded against unauthorised code execution (PW.5.1, p. 16). Secure model serialisation and capture of build tool versions for provenance are considerations (PW.6, p. 16). Code review and analysis policies should include AI model code, and all models should be scanned for malware, vulnerabilities and backdoors (PW.7, pp. 16–17). Testing policies should include AI models, and the forms of testing usable for them include unit, integration and penetration testing, red teaming, use case testing and adversarial testing, with automating tests as regression tests a consideration, and models retested when retrained or given new data sources (PW.8, p. 17). Secure-by-default settings carry only a note on documenting settings early (PW.9, p. 17).

## Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV)

All model inputs and outputs should be logged, monitored and analysed for security and performance issues; users of AI models (here, system producers and acquirers) should be made aware of how to report issues and of their inherent limitations; vulnerability and incident databases should be watched for AI-related concerns, including machine learning frameworks and libraries; and models should be scanned and tested frequently, mainly by automation with a human in the loop as needed, and audited periodically (RV.1, pp. 17–18). Vulnerability analysis may include deep analysis of model input and output for deviations from normal behaviour (RV.2.1, p. 18). Risk responses should weigh the time and cost of rebuilding a model, and organisations should set criteria and processes for when to stop using a model and roll back, and consider being ready to stop at any time and carry on by other means until its risks are sufficiently addressed (RV.2.2, pp. 18–19). Being able to review training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data after the fact can help identify some root causes; the remaining root-cause tasks carry no AI-specific additions (RV.3, p. 19).

## Glossary

The glossary defines nine terms, mostly from EO 14110: artificial intelligence, AI model, AI red-teaming (a structured testing effort to find flaws and vulnerabilities in an AI system), AI system, data science, dual-use foundation model (trained on broad data, generally self-supervised, at least tens of billions of parameters, and exhibiting, or easily modified to exhibit, high performance at tasks posing serious risks, such as lowering barriers to CBRN weapons, enabling powerful offensive cyber operations against a wide range of potential targets, or evading human control), generative AI, model weight, and provenance (metadata on the origination or source of data) (p. 22).

## Key Statistics

- 20 practices and 48 tasks in Table 1: PO 14, PS 6, PW 19, RV 9 (tally of Table 1 rows, pp. 8–19, counted for the deep reference; the Profile states no totals).
- Priorities: 21 High, 22 Medium, 5 Low (same tally).
- 10 tasks with no AI-specific additions; 6 tasks and the PW.3 practice new to the Profile; 3 tasks and the PO.5 and PS.1 practices modified from SSDF 1.1 (same tally).
- Dual-use foundation models: at least tens of billions of parameters (p. 22).
- EO 14110 Section 4.1.a; NIST workshop January 2024; approved 2024-07-25 (pp. 1, ii; PDF p. 3).

## Key Connections

- Executive Order 14110: the tasking, the definition of dual-use foundation models the Audience relies on, and seven of the nine glossary definitions (pp. i, ii, 1, 22).
- NIST SP 800-218, SSDF Version 1.1: the base the Profile supplements and must be used with (pp. 1, 6, 8).
- NIST AI RMF 1.0, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1, and NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2e2023): the three informative-reference sources (p. 7).
- NIST resources listed for other risks include the AI RMF Playbook, the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1), the bias standard SP 1270, SP 800-161r1, the Privacy Framework and IR 8286 (p. 5).
- CSF 2.0, SP 800-53 and Dioptra: among the sources of expertise; EO 14028: the SSDF has been used in its support (p. 2).
- SBOM and SLSA as vehicles for provenance data (PS.3.2, p. 13).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. The Profile is not a checklist; it is a risk-based starting point to adapt (p. 4).
2. The Profile is not to be used without SP 800-218 (pp. 1, 8).
3. Human-written and AI-generated source code are not treated differently; all source code is to be evaluated before use (p. 2).
